clinicalPearls: Consider AIH in any patient with unexplained acute or chronic hepatocellular injury, especially young to middle-aged women, but it can occur at any age and in either sex.
Presentation is highly variable, from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant acute liver failure or established cirrhosis at diagnosis.
Marked hypergammaglobulinemia (especially elevated IgG) out of proportion to the degree of liver injury is a classic clue.
Two broad serologic patterns exist: type 1 (ANA and/or anti-smooth-muscle antibody positive) and type 2 (anti-LKM1 positive, more common in children).
Concurrent autoimmune conditions (autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, ulcerative colitis) support the diagnosis.
Liver biopsy showing interface hepatitis with a dense plasma cell infiltrate is characteristic and helps confirm diagnosis and grade severity.
A dramatic biochemical response to immunosuppressive therapy is itself supportive of the diagnosis and is used as a diagnostic criterion when the picture is ambiguous.
Overlap syndromes with primary biliary cholangitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis occur and should be considered when cholestatic features coexist.
harrison.pathophysiology: AIH results from a breakdown in immune self-tolerance leading to T-cell-mediated attack on hepatocytes in a genetically susceptible host, often triggered by an environmental factor such as a viral infection or drug exposure. Autoantibody production (ANA, anti-smooth-muscle antibody, or anti-LKM1) accompanies the T-cell-driven injury but is thought to be a marker rather than the primary mediator of hepatocyte damage. Chronic interface hepatitis with ongoing necroinflammation can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis if untreated.
additionalDifferentials: Viral hepatitis (acute or chronic hepatitis B or C)
infectionMimics: Acute viral hepatitis A, B, C, or E
nonInfectiousMimics: Primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis overlap
additionalInvestigations: ANA and anti-smooth-muscle antibody — supports type 1 AIH diagnosis
Anti-LKM1 antibody — supports type 2 AIH, more typical in pediatric cases
Serum IgG level — characteristic hypergammaglobulinemia aids diagnosis and monitoring
Liver biopsy — confirms interface hepatitis and plasma cell infiltrate, stages fibrosis
Viral hepatitis serologies (hepatitis B and C) — exclude viral etiology
Ceruloplasmin and copper studies — exclude Wilson disease, especially in younger patients
Alkaline phosphatase and antimitochondrial antibody — screen for overlap with primary biliary cholangitis
Standardized AIH scoring system (simplified diagnostic criteria) — integrates autoantibodies, IgG, histology, and viral exclusion
redFlags: Acute presentation with coagulopathy or encephalopathy suggesting evolution to acute liver failure
Jaundice with rapidly rising bilirubin and synthetic dysfunction
Evidence of established cirrhosis or portal hypertension at initial presentation
Lack of biochemical response after an adequate trial of immunosuppression, raising concern for an alternate or overlapping diagnosis
Signs of decompensation (ascites, variceal bleeding) warranting hepatology and transplant center referral
pitfalls: Attributing transaminase elevation solely to another cause (e.g., fatty liver or medication) without considering AIH, delaying treatment
Relying on autoantibody titers alone; seronegative AIH exists, and titers do not reliably track disease activity
Missing an overlap syndrome with cholestatic liver disease when only hepatocellular pattern is evaluated
Discontinuing therapy too early without confirming sustained biochemical and histologic remission, risking relapse
harrison.prognosis: With timely immunosuppressive treatment, most patients achieve biochemical remission and have a favorable long-term prognosis, though relapse after treatment withdrawal is common and many require long-term maintenance therapy. Untreated or refractory disease can progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, and the need for liver transplantation.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Autoimmune Hepatitis chapter (Chronic Hepatitis section)
